speaker_label: Professor RON WALTERS (University of Maryland; Author; Adviser to Jesse      Jackson's Presidential Campaigns)

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Pastor, Christ Evangelical Lutheran Church;      Adviser to President Bush's 2004 Reelection Campaign)

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Head, Christ Evangelical Lutheran Church,      Philadelphia)
text: I don't think there's any sense of panic.  Obviously,      there's--it's not a fun day when you have these kinds of issues to      contend with.  I think every one of the people that you've talked about      expects to be cleared of any charges that have been leveled against them.      And the hope is that once these charges have cleared that we can carry      on with the agenda of this party and this president.

Joe Watkins, let's switch topics for a second and go to      Harriet Miers, the president's nominee to replace Sandra Day O'Connor on      the Supreme Court.  The angry response, the sense of disappointment, is      not coming from the left.  It's coming from the right.  Why?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Head, Christ Evangelical Lutheran Church,      Philadelphia)

Donna Brazile, Democrats, on the other hand, seem rather      positive, at least in terms of the politicians on Capitol Hill, in a      response to the Miers nomination.  Harry Reid, the Democrat leader in the      Senate, has said, `I like Harriet Miers.'  That disappointed some on the      left.  Are you disappointed?

Look, I think beyond what we've learned in the paper that      she's well-qualified, that she broke the glass ceiling, we need to know      if she will uphold individual rights and liberties and what type of judge      she will become. speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Head, Christ Evangelical Lutheran Church,      Philadelphia)

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Head, Christ Evangelical Lutheran Church,      Philadelphia)

Gentlemen, thank you for joining us.
Good to be with you.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Head, Christ Evangelical Lutheran Church)
text: Nice      to be here, Juan.

Topic one, President Bush nominated Samuel Alito Jr. as his      nominee for the Supreme Court.  He's touted his qualifications, having      attended Princeton and Yale.  Why there was no minority or woman      considered to replace Sandra Day O'Connor on the court--were you      surprised, Reverend Watkins, that none of these people ended up on the      short list to replace Harriet Miers once her nomination failed?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Head, Christ Evangelical Lutheran Church)
text: Well, it seemed to me that the president was more      interested in doing the right thing, which is appointing the best person      for that position and somebody who it would be very, very hard for people      on either side of the aisle to dispute.  Samuel Alito is that kind of a      candidate, and obviously there are lots of great candidates--Hispanic      candidates, African-American candidates, male candidates, female      candidates--a lot of outstanding people out there that this president      could have chosen.  He made a great pick, however, in Samuel Alito, and      I'm pleased with it.
And, Ron Walters, what do you think about the absence of women      or minorities on the final list?

Well, Ron, what this speaks loudly to is that diversity      really was not a value that the people he was trying to please cared very      much about.  He was--and let's be clear--he was trying to please the      conservative base to the Republican Party.  President Bush really needs      this wing of the party given the fact that his favorability ratings are      so low.  He needs them to govern. Let's move on to another topic, which is Lewis "Scooter"      Libby, the vice president's chief of staff, being indicted on five counts      of obstruction of justice, perjury in the investigation by a special      prosecutor into the leak of a CIA agent's identity.  Joe Watkins, do you      think that Scooter Libby's going to strike a plea deal?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Head, Christ Evangelical Lutheran Church)
text: Well, it's possible that Scooter Libby could strike a plea      deal.  I mean, he his easily a very, very busy guy.  And, truth be told,      with any busy official in the White House, especially any chief of staff      to a vice president or to a US president--with all the stuff that they      have coming at them--I know that I was a staffer at the White House, and      I was not nearly as busy as a chief of staff or a deputy chief of staff,      and my plate was full.  I couldn't return all the phone calls that I had,      and it's very, very possible that Scooter Libby could have in a      non-malicious way been mistaken about when it is he first learned of      Valerie Plame's name.
If Joe Watkins was your defense attorney, Ron Walters, would      you be a happy man?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Head, Christ Evangelical Lutheran Church)
text: I'm sure not!

I'm afraid not.  What we know, and we know fairly clearly      from the investigation, is that Vice President Cheney told Robert Novak      that Valerie Plame was a CIA agent, and what we also know is that the      relationship between he and Scooter Libby, they're extremely close.  They      ride to work together.  It's inconceivable to me to think that Scooter      Libby would have gone off on a solo project.  All we can say is that      Libby was indicted on a technicality and that in some respects Patrick      Fitzgerald did not have the courage to go after the vice president.

Now let's go on to a subject that's closely tied to this,      which was the effort by the Democrats in the Senate--successful effort to      close the Senate on Tuesday to allow for questioning about weapons of      mass destruction and why the Senate Intelligence Committee, led by      Senator Pat Roberts, Republican of Kansas, has not produced a report on      whether or not the administration exaggerated reports on weapons of mass      destruction in order to justify going to war in Iraq.  Joe Watkins, did      you see this as a stunt, which is what Senator Bill Frist, the majority      leader, described it as?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Head, Christ Evangelical Lutheran Church)
text: I think Senator Frist described it accurately, which is      that it's a kind of a counterpunch strategy, which is to say that they      have not really put forward to the American people an agenda of their      own, saying, `These are our values, these are the things about which we      care deeply, and this is where we hope to head.' Ron Walters, did you think that the Democratic maneuver--or      stunt, as Senator Frist called it--was effective?

I do think it was effective because the president, of      course, was attempting to get the Libby indictment off of the front pages      of the newspapers and out of the talk shows.  And then, of course, the      Democrats said, `Well, let's get this back in the public eye,' and that      was the source of the dramatic attempt to do that.  I mean, this is      extremely serious. Welcome, Reverend Watkins.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Pastor, Christ Evangelical Lutheran Church)

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Pastor, Christ Evangelical Lutheran Church)
text: Very, very comfortable.  Very, very good.  I think he gave      a very, very good speech and it was very honest. The fact that--despite the fact that there has been some faulty      information, we are making tremendous progress. Do you think that the president adequately expressed what we      need to leave in Iraq?  If the US is eventually going to pull out troops,      what kind of state do we need to leave in that nation?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Pastor, Christ Evangelical Lutheran Church)
text: Well, I think he wants to make sure that before we leave      that the Iraqis are able to maintain the peace that we've fought so hard      to bring them.  And I think that's happening and the president talked      about that in his speech last night.  It's important that we not cut and      run, which is what some of the defeatists, as he called them, are saying,      that because of the fact that there have been all these sad images in the      news media of people dying so tragically that now it's time to just get      out right away and leave behind whatever we've got there.  Well, that      wouldn't be fair.  That wouldn't be fulfilling our promise to the Iraqi      people.  And that certainly would be minimizing the sacrifice of all the      people who've gone before who've given their lives for the sake of      freedom and democracy in Iraq.  I think the president set out in very      clear terms what we're trying to do, about helping the Iraqi government      establish the institutions that they need to be a--to have a unified and      lasting democracy and to make sure that all of Iraq's people--and they      have different groups as you know--are included and represented.
As a pastor, how do you deal with questions from your flock      about this war in particular, the cost of death in any war and just      guiding them through thinking about current events?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Pastor, Christ Evangelical Lutheran Church)
text: Well, for the most part, I think that folks      know--certainly if the Scriptures are the authoritative book for the      people in my congregation, they know that there's both an Old Testament      and a New Testament and war is nothing new to our world, nothing new to      people.  There are have been wars and conflicts since the beginning of      time, and sadly, people have given their lives in war for the sake of      others.  And this, of course, is a very, very difficult thing to      comprehend, to understand, to reconcile for all people, certainly for      people of faith.  But, nonetheless, I'm encouraged every single time I      hear of brave American men and women of different ethnicities talking      about the importance of being there, the importance of the mission.      We've got a number of people who have been involved in the military      service and who have spent time in Afghanistan and Iraq and who say that      we're not only winning but we're doing the right thing--they're there for      the right reason and that what's happening is a good thing.  And the      biggest challenge that a lot of military people who are there have is      wondering why more American people don't support the mission, especially      since they're there on the ground seeing what's going on.

You speak about a lack of support for the mission.  And, in      fact, there's an almost historic low among African-Americans of support      for this particular war.  What do you see as the reasons, and do you      think the president's speech addressed some of those questions      specifically in the African-American community?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Pastor, Christ Evangelical Lutheran Church)

Juan.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group at Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: It's really not at all about that. There are people on both sides of the isle who, from time to time, have problems. And this is a problem that Congressman Jefferson has. speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group at Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: And that's really - well, it's just hard to refute that kind of stuff, when you've got videotape evidence of him doing that. It's going to be very, very hard for Congressman Jefferson. speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group at Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: Now, he's even got Republicans who are, not necessarily on his side, but who have problems with some of the ways that some of the searches that have been conducted in the past. Nobody holds Jack Abramoff's background, his religion against him or Tom DeLay's. But in this situation, with a black congressman, race does seem to become a factor, Reverend Watkins.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group at Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: Well, this is a very, very sad thing, a very unfortunate thing. I don't think, however, that this is a conspiracy. That - I think that when charges are leveled, it's because the authorities have done months and months and months of investigation. And the investigations just take time to unfold, and when they become public, generally speaking, they have everything in place to bring the charges forward.

speaker_label: Professor RON WALTERS (Professor of Political Science, University of Maryland; Author, "Freedom is Not Enough")
text: But Juan, you know, there are a couple of questions here remaining. One is that if they do have such drop-dead evidence, as a video, why was it then that they went into a congressman's congressional office? I mean, that is, seems to me that there's a case here that maybe, yes, as Reverend Watkins says, unfolding. But it seems to me, that if have uncontroversial evidence, why go to the extreme measures of going into his office?

speaker_label: Professor RON WALTERS (Professor of Political Science, University of Maryland; Author, "Freedom is Not Enough")
text: The other thing is that, people point out that no one has gone into Tom DeLay's office. And so this looks like, sort of selective treatment on the part, of an African-American member of congress.

speaker_label: Professor RON WALTERS (Professor of Political Science, University of Maryland; Author, "Freedom is Not Enough")
text: In any case, the culture of corruption charge, yes, I think it's been a political point on the part of the Republican Party to try to prove that the culture of corruption spans both ways. And giving this a high profile is another one of those ways that they kick up Jefferson, into that pile. And then they're able to make that argument.
On this point, does that excuse the idea that he has been videotaped, taking this money?

speaker_label: Professor RON WALTERS (Professor of Political Science, University of Maryland; Author, "Freedom is Not Enough")
text: We haven't gone into the merits of the case. I'm not there yet.
Okay.

speaker_label: Professor RON WALTERS (Professor of Political Science, University of Maryland; Author, "Freedom is Not Enough")
text: But let me say, because when you get to the merits of the case, you have to consider also the context of the people. Last year, I was in Dallas, at a literary festival for my book. Every member of the City Council who was black was under investigation.

speaker_label: Professor RON WALTERS (Professor of Political Science, University of Maryland; Author, "Freedom is Not Enough")
text: Now that is compiled a long record of the harassment of black elected officials. Congressman Mervyn Dymally put out a report when he was in the Congress and showed this massive use of the investigative power of law enforcement officials, was at the national and state level. speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member of Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll)

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member of Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll)

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member of Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll)

speaker_label: Ms. DONNA BRAZILE (Democratic Political Consultant; Former Campaign Manager for Democratic Presidential Nominee Al Gore)

speaker_label: Ms. DONNA BRAZILE (Democratic Political Consultant; Former Campaign Manager for Democratic Presidential Nominee Al Gore)

speaker_label: Ms. DONNA BRAZILE (Democratic Political Consultant; Former Campaign Manager for Democratic Presidential Nominee Al Gore)

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member of Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll)

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member of Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll)

Thanks, Ed. We're joined now on Political Corner by Ron Walters, professor of political science at the University of Maryland. Professor Walters' latest book is called Freedom is Not Enough. Reverend Watkins was a member of the first President Bush's White House staff. He joins us from NPR's bureau in New York. And today, I'm at NPR's bureau in Chicago.

Gentlemen, let's begin Political Corner by talking about same-sex marriage. The president, as you know, has been out urging an amendment to ban same sex marriage. It's not seen as having much of a chance of being approved. But on Tuesday, outside the Russell Senate Office Building, you saw black ministers standing next to the likes of Congresswoman Katherine Harris, next to Senator Wayne Allard, the Republican from Colorado, all condemning same-sex marriage.
Joe Watkins, is it being done out of a sincere feeling that this is, you know, a cultural moment when you have to say no to gay marriage?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group at Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: Well, it's even bigger than politics as you can see, because a lot of the ministers that may have been standing with Katherine Harris and various other well known Republican legislators may not classify themselves are Republicans. But they certainly agree with the Republican Party and with this president on this issue.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group at Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: And it shows that the Republican Party has the ability to attract African-Americans who agree with them on a lot of the values issues. So this is a very, very strong signal. We saw this, of course, in some states back in 2004. During that election cycle you saw in Ohio and Florida and various other places, African-American ministers who may, in the past, not have aligned with the Democratic Party, aligning with the president and Republicans in that election because they agree with Republicans on that important issue.
Ron Walters, though, is this a dangerous sign, another dangerous signal for Democrats going into the mid-term elections?

speaker_label: Professor RON WALTERS (Professor of Political Science, University of Maryland)
text: Not at all. This is an opportunity, at least, to turn the page, to divert the discussion, to change the mood of the American people to something else. When you look at the casualties continuing to amount in Iraq and other kinds of problems that Americans having, this is sort of a cynical ploy to change the politics and the mood of what people are talking about right now.

Gentlemen, let me take you into the White House press briefing room on Tuesday for an interesting exchange that took place between CBS News's Bill Plante and the new White House spokesman, Tony Snow. Tony Snow, in talking about the same-sex marriage amendment proposal, said it was the same thing - he equated it with the civil rights bills that were enacted in the 1960s. Bill Plante said you would say that that's the equal with civil rights, speaking about the union between a man and a man and woman and a woman.

And Tony Snow said, well, no, it's your question. And then he said he needed to get a more precise definition. Joe Watkins, is this being advanced as the same thing as African-Americans having their civil rights put into law?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group at Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: As an African-American who certainly has benefited the hard work of so many people during the 1950s and 1960s to level the playing field in this country, I don't know that anything can equate with that. Every issue is what it is, and it's own issue.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group at Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: This is an important one because, obviously, it has something to do with the way families look in this country going forward. It's not against anybody, but it's really more a statement for families, for the institution of marriage. And I grew up in a traditional family. I was so fortunate to have my mother and a father, and I still do.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group at Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: And my parents raised me with the understanding that marriage is between a man and woman. That's not to say anything about contracts between people or other kinds of things. But it certainly does say that marriage, the institution as we know it and as we understand it, and certainly as the Bible has ordained it, is between a man and a woman.

All right, gentlemen, one last topic. This is such an interesting concept. What you had here is a proposition that there should be a unity campaign for the presidency for the White House in 2008, joining a Republican and a Democrat on the ticket to try to end the polarized politics in America. What do you think of this? I mean, does it have any realistic chances? Is it a pipe dream, Ron Walters?

speaker_label: Professor RON WALTERS (Professor of Political Science, University of Maryland)
text: The question for me is, who will this hurt? Now, these two have concluded that there needs to be a union between Democrats and Republicans. And what they're going to try to do is to have an election by Internet where they have both a Republican and a Democrat on the ticket.

speaker_label: Professor RON WALTERS (Professor of Political Science, University of Maryland)
text: Now, that's extraordinary. Pipe dream, maybe, Juan, but it's going to be very difficult to pull off.
Joe Watkins, what do you think?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group at Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: I think their intention is good, but I don't think that it's at all feasible. I don't think it can work. It's brand new, it's Internet-based. And that sounds maybe exciting to some people. But remember that if it is Internet-based it's going to knock out a whole segment of voters. Particularly, poor people - which is nearly a quarter of the American populous - who don't have access to the Internet. So those people wouldn't even be able to participate in this kind of a process.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group at Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: So, to me, I don't think that it really has legs.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member of Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll; Member of the First President Bush's White House Staff)
text: And that's part of the reason why you see the Democrats leading the parade to have the congressman stripped of his committee post here. speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member of Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll; Member of the First President Bush's White House Staff)

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member of Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll; Member of the First President Bush's White House Staff)

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member of Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll; Member of the First President Bush's White House Staff)

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member of Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll; Member of the First President Bush's White House Staff)

I mean, you know, they were like positioned in areas where there's hardly any homeowners back in the neighborhood. So I applaud both the mayor and the governor for making this decision. This is a good decision. The Orleans Parish Police Department, they're under a lot of pressure now, the fire department, to try to rebuild its ranks. And at the time when we're trying to do all of that, I think it's important that, you know, the mayor and the governor get the essential help they need to tamp down on this crime before it gets overblown this summer.

Rev. Watkins, it's now almost one year since the hurricane blew through and the political consequences, as they've played out here in Washington, seem very interesting. It seems as if at this point there's a consensus that the Bush Administration feels this happened on their watch, and they are going to try to do all they can to repair. Is that right?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: I think that's right. I think the president - what I really admire about his position on all this is that the buck stops with him. And it's not about assigning blame to anybody else, but it's a matter of looking at what we can do, since it happened under our watch, to get things done and to bring about positive change.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: And it doesn't have to do with Republican or Democrat either. It's about making sure that Americans everywhere, and specifically Americans in the areas that were most hard - that were hit most hard, get the satisfaction that they need. So he's working very, very hard, and has a number of his agencies working very, very hard to provide satisfaction.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: And I'm really pleased with the - some of the bipartisan stuff that's happened, some of the bipartisan work that's been done to make - to bring about positive change.

Well, one of the things that has made the news recently is that some of the people who were given emergency spending money use it on things like Girls Gone Wild and other kinds of frivolities. Is that going to undermine support for future spending on recovery in the Gulf Coast region, and especially to people in need, Rev. Watkins?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: I don't think it'll undermine it. I just think that people will be a lot more careful in the future as to how dollars are spent and where money is going. Obviously, because resources are so scarce, you want to make sure that every dollar that's allocated goes some place where it's needed and that it's not being ill spent or poorly spent.
Well...
You know, Juan, I...
Donna Brazile, are you worried about that issue?

Absolutely. Look, it - right now, the current projection's up to possibly $2 billion. That is just an absurd amount of money to have slipped out of the hands of the people who really desperately need it to rebuild their homes and to get back on their feet.

And when you hear that prisoners - I mean God knows, somebody should have checked the P.O. box and said oh, wait a minute, it's going to a prison. I mean, when you hear that prisoners were able to get $2,000 debit cards - we must have proper safeguards and procedures so that we do not lose one nickel of this money. This is so important to the people...

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: Absolutely.
...coming back. And they need this money. And to have a couple of you know, and, Rev. Watkins, you probably...

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: Bad apples.

One last question on this topic: where do we stand in terms of delivering on the promise of fully funding that recovery, and is it sufficient? Donna, why don't you begin?

Well, let me just, first of all, applaud both the president and the Congress for keeping their word to help us rebuild, in terms of the resources needed to rebuild the levees. When I sat down with President Bush, along with others last year, there was $1.3 billion in the budget. Today, over $3 billion have been allocated to restore the levees. I want to say thank you to everybody who's been involved. Chairman Don Powell has done a fantastic job.

Now, the president also committed to giving us about $10 billion in homeowner assistance. That's for the state of Louisiana. We now have the money; it's in the bank, and the process is underway. And this summer, homeowners will get that money, so we're pleased with that. There's also additional money for restoring the colleges and universities, money to begin the restoring some of the hospitals, the roads, the transportation, the infrastructure. There's also money from FEMA to remove all of the cars that have been - that were abandoned after Katrina.

So I'm going to say thank you to not just to Congress and the president, but to the American people for their patience and for their generosity in helping us, you know, have the resources necessary to begin the rebuilding.

But here's the problem: we now need a plan in New Orleans. We got to figure out what neighborhoods can be restored, what the requirements are to rebuild those homes. You know, we got new, strict building codes. And we need to help homeowners find their way back home. And there's a toll free number. It's 1-888-762-3252. That is the number that people can call so that they can, you know, get this homeowners assistance and begin to rebuild.

Joe Watkins, you know, that sounds like good news, a good report from Donna Brazile. But on the front page of The New York Times recently I saw that FEMA is spending like millions to just hold onto some trailers in Arkansas that should have been designated for use to help storm recovery victims in Louisiana and Mississippi. Is there a sense that some of this money is just going up in smoke?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: Well, obviously, as Donna said, the - we've all got to be more careful. There's got to be a lot more scrutiny with regards to how these precious dollars are spent. We want to make sure that the money that's being allocated gets to the people who really need it. That's what it's all about.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: And this is - there is a complete bipartisan sense of this. This is not about partisan politics. It's about making sure that the people who have been put in harm's way and who have really suffered because of what happened there get the help that they need.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll)
text: No matter what happens, clearly, there is resolve on the part of both Democrats and Republicans to get it done, to make sure that the people in that part of the country get the aid that they need. And it's all about helping Americans, really. That's what it's about.
But, (unintelligible)...
Joe Watkins, let me move - I'm sorry.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney)
text: Well, of course, candidates say things during the heat of the campaigns and during quiet moments when they may have their guard down. speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney)

Donna Brazile, but it does look, at least from, you know, an outsider looking in, as if Michael Steele is biting the hand that's been feeding him, that's been lifting him up in terms of political circles. What's going on?

On the other hand, I think it has everything to do with poll numbers, and he doesn't want to go down a sinking ship.

Well, if President Bush is not going to go campaign for Michael Steele because Michael Steele doesn't want to be too close to him, the president does have a welcome mat extended from Pennsylvania gubernatorial nominee Lynn Swann, again a Republican, a black Republican.
Joe Watkins, why does Lynn Swann want President Bush coming into Pennsylvania?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney)
text: Well, Lynn Swann is a great candidate. The only thing that he lacks right now is really the money that he needs to be able to compete with Ed Rendell in the fall campaign. And what he goes on to say is that you still have an administration that does things like politicize the Civil Rights Division of the Justice Department, a president that is all for repealing a estate tax and high taxes but not paying attention to issues of poverty in the country.
So, Donna Brazile, is Paul Krugman right? Is that the reason that black Americans, despite the Michael Steeles and the Lynn Swanns, still don't believe that the president is worth their vote?

It took Democrats over 40 years to attract the black support that it currently enjoys. And I think for Republicans, they have to come to grips with the fact that many African-Americans have been turned off by their lack of follow through.
When do you think that there will be a competition for the black vote?

I think it will come when there's a serious person running for the presidency that somehow (unintelligible) make an overture to African-Americans throughout the process. I think it will come over years of African-Americans hearing from Republican presidents and Republican Congress and Republican governors that African-Americans are wanted, that African-Americans will have a seat at the table to help shape public policy.

But we're a long way from that period. Right now what we have is we have good African-Americans who are serving in the Bush administration. We have excellent black candidates who are running for public office for the first time. So this is the beginning of a period that will take many years for the Republicans to enjoy black support.
Joe Watkins, do you think Donna Brazile is being pragmatic, or is she daydreaming?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney)

Not perhaps as quickly as some people on the Republican side might like to see them change, but they are changing. There is certainly in some circles a greater interest and more awareness of the Republican Party for African-Americans.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney)
text: And this is good. We saw it, of course, in the 2004 election, and we're likely to see it again this coming November. I think the Republicans will be able to capitalize in some of the disappointment that African-Americans have had with Democrats taking them for granted in some instances. And they'll look more closely at Republicans.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney)

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Member, Government Relations Group, Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney)

speaker_label: Professor RON WALTERS (Political Science, University of Maryland, Author, Freedom is Not Enough)

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Associate Director of Government Relations, Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney)
text: In the state of Louisiana, of course, we've consistently, since the beginning, engaged or seen an engagement of the blame game. Why is there no mention of the governor in this? Why is there no mention of the responsibility of state officials and the need for city and state officials to work better in this incident?

There is something behind this more than simply ineptitude. There's a lot of high politics behind this, and there is still a desire on the part of a lot of people to use this money to change New Orleans the way they want to see it changed. And I've been down there several times, especially around the election.

And listening to people in the business community talk about the new New Orleans - and they really want a New Orleans that has a very strongly beefed up tourist sector as the basis of its economic development - for those people, they obviously want a lot of the people who are stuck in the mire of poverty in the 9th Ward and other places, they want them gone.

They want enough of them to remain - and one time that I went down there I had a very long discussion with a restaurant - a white restaurant owner - they want enough of them to stay so they can work in the restaurants. But the normal resident, that's - for poor residents, that quite another issue.

Reverend Joseph Watkins, part of the government relations group at Buchanan Ingersoll, a former aide to the first President Bush. speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Associate Director of Government Relations, Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney)

I'm joined now by Donna Brazile, former campaign manager for Democratic presidential nominee Al Gore in the 2000 presidential campaign. Reverend Watkins was a member of the first President Bush's White House staff. Donna, Joe Watkins, what do you think about Deval Patrick? Now we have a black governor, the second black governor, I suppose, since Reconstruction, but almost nobody pays attention to this fact. He doesn't get the kind of celebration that had attended Doug Wilder when Wilder was governor of Virginia. What's going on, Donna Brazile?

speaker_label: Ms. DONNA BRAZILE (Political Consultant; Former Campaign Manager for Al Gore)
text: Oh, I think Deval took over the Commonwealth of Massachusetts at a time when the state is having some difficulty with its budget. He has tried to put in place, you know, new people to get the state back on its feet. And I think with the revelation recently regarding Deval's interference of, you know, perhaps making a phone call on behalf of a former client, he got into a little controversy.

speaker_label: Ms. DONNA BRAZILE (Political Consultant; Former Campaign Manager for Al Gore)
text: And just recently, his wife, First Lady Diane Patrick announced - well, the governor's office announced in a statement that she is being treated for exhaustion and depression. The governor also announced that he will work on a flexible schedule for the next couple of weeks in order to spend more time with his family. He has delegated some of his duties to the Lieutenant Governor Tim Murphy, and, of course, the cabinet.

Well, now, Joe, according to this study by the University of North Carolina, he's the most powerful governor in the country because Democrats control both the governorship and the state house for the first time in 16 years, making it a veto-proof majority in case he wants to get any legislation, any budget through the legislature. But at the moment, it doesn't seem to make a difference if he's not there, if he's dealing with personal problems.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Government Relations Firm, Buchanan, Ingersoll and Rooney)
text: There is no doubt about that, and he has to get past his personal problems, of course, so that he can get on track, though, with being the governor of Massachusetts.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Government Relations Firm, Buchanan, Ingersoll and Rooney)
text: And also, there's the added pressure on him, of course, of being in a situation where he has this veto-proof majority in the legislator, in both chambers. There's going to be a lot of pressure on him to really show what he has accomplished in the four years that he's been governor.

Well, Donna, let's take listeners back just a step here. What was it that allowed Deval Patrick to win in Massachusetts? And because I wanted just everyone want to know here - putting it in perspective - that Mitt Romney, you know, a conservative Republican now running for president on the GOP side, was his predecessor. So how can the state's voters go from electing Mitt Romney to electing Deval Patrick?

speaker_label: Ms. DONNA BRAZILE (Political Consultant; Former Campaign Manager for Al Gore)
text: Well, the lieutenant governor, Ms. Healey, ran a very weak campaign. Governor Patrick ran from Day One, although he was in a congested Democratic primary, he ran a grassroots campaign. He connected with voters. Voters felt comfortable with his leadership, and he won overwhelmingly in, of course, in a Democratic-leaning state.

speaker_label: Ms. DONNA BRAZILE (Political Consultant; Former Campaign Manager for Al Gore)
text: I think Ms. Healy made some very important errors. She ran some campaign ads featuring a white woman going into a - look like a tunnel, a garage, with a grainy backdrop and suggested that governor - well, at the time - Deval Patrick would be weak on crime. It backfired, and it caused voters to seriously question her judgment. And Deval Patrick won with over 20 percent of the vote - more than 20 percent of the vote.

speaker_label: Ms. DONNA BRAZILE (Political Consultant; Former Campaign Manager for Al Gore)
text: So I think it was not an easy campaign. He had to fight for it. He was a good candidate. And clearly, Governor Patrick now must focus on getting the government fit to function better. Governor - the former government Romney left with a strong disapproval rating. People - while he's running for president, voters in Massachusetts gave him an overwhelming negative approval rating. So Governor Patrick has an opportunity to turn things around.
Joe Watkins, I want to hear your version of this story. Why did he win handily, given that his predecessor was Mitt Romney, a conservative Republican?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Government Relations Firm, Buchanan, Ingersoll and Rooney)
text: Well, he - I think the voters judged the candidates based on who they are and what they'll do at the time. And Mitt Romney, of course, was elected governor of Massachusetts. He did a great job as governor, and he has - he's in a very good position right now as a candidate for the presidency of the United States - for the Republican nomination, that is. I think he's going to be a very, very strong candidate in that regard.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Government Relations Firm, Buchanan, Ingersoll and Rooney)
text: But I think Deval Patrick ran a very good race. And I think Donna Brazile said it right, that he ran a very, very strong grassroots campaign. He talked to the voters. The good thing that it says about voters in this Commonwealth of Massachusetts is that they're much bigger than color. That they looked at the candidates and they voted for candidates based upon how they felt about what they're saying, not based on the color of their skin.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Government Relations Firm, Buchanan, Ingersoll and Rooney)
text: That's a wonderful statement for all of America that that kind of thing is happening now in this country. We had a great candidate in Lieutenant Governor Healey. She came up short on Election Day and Deval Patrick won a very, very strong race.

One last question on this topic, Donna and Joe, which is does he fit in with the likes of Harold Ford, Barack Obama sort of new generation black politics? What does he stand for? What does he say is his calling card in terms of his agenda?

speaker_label: Ms. DONNA BRAZILE (Political Consultant; Former Campaign Manager for Al Gore)
text: Well, if you look at his inaugural speech, I thought he gave one of the best inaugural speeches of all of the newly-elected governor. He's an optimist. He's someone who comes from a long tradition of fighting for social justice. He hails from Illinois, where he grew up on the south side of Chicago.

speaker_label: Ms. DONNA BRAZILE (Political Consultant; Former Campaign Manager for Al Gore)
text: In his state of the state speech, he talked about the poor, the young. He talked about public schools that often fail poor kids. He talked about building hope in hospitals and in community centers. And he talked about using the great strength of the people of Massachusetts to help the least of these.

speaker_label: Ms. DONNA BRAZILE (Political Consultant; Former Campaign Manager for Al Gore)
text: So I think the jury is still out on - clearly, he's gotten off to a very difficult beginning, but I know Deval Patrick personally. And knowing this good man, I know he will turn things around and get back on his feet.
And you should have mentioned, I think, that he was also head of the Civil Rights Division at the Justice Department under President Clinton.

speaker_label: Ms. DONNA BRAZILE (Political Consultant; Former Campaign Manager for Al Gore)
text: That is correct.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Government Relations Firm, Buchanan, Ingersoll and Rooney)
text: Right.

speaker_label: Ms. DONNA BRAZILE (Political Consultant; Former Campaign Manager for Al Gore)
text: And he had a exemplary career there and well respected by both sides of the House.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Government Relations Firm, Buchanan, Ingersoll and Rooney)
text: But he…
Joe Watkins, do you see him fitting in with this kind of new generation black political leadership? Or is he of some other school, and exactly what does he stand for in your mind?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Government Relations Firm, Buchanan, Ingersoll and Rooney)
text: All three of them are a great candidates and certainly leaders of the future, you - Harold Ford, Barack Obama and Deval Patrick - but three very different candidates, three very different politicians.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Government Relations Firm, Buchanan, Ingersoll and Rooney)
text: Harold Ford, of course, much more conservative politically than the others. Somebody who openly talked about his faith on the campaign in Tennessee, ran a very, very strong race for the U.S. Senate in Tennessee, and he's somebody who I'm sure will be back given the fact that he's got this great position now, I believe, with Merrill Lynch. That'll be a great springboard for him if ever he wants to run again for political office statewide or nationally.

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Government Relations Firm, Buchanan, Ingersoll and Rooney)
text: Barack Obama, of course, his story is being made, as we speak. And right now, he's still in the honeymoon period with Americans as they get to know him better. But he'll have to answer to some of the tougher questions about his voting record as a member of the Illinois State Senate, and also talk more clearly and specifically about where he'd like to take America as it relates to the war in Iraq and domestic issues.
By the way, on that voting record, what are you referring to?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Government Relations Firm, Buchanan, Ingersoll and Rooney)
text: I'm referring to the fact that when he was a member of the Illinois State Senate, on several occasions, he voted - he chose to vote present on some very, very important issues. And that something he's going to have answer…
Such as?

speaker_label: Reverend JOSEPH WATKINS (Government Relations Firm, Buchanan, Ingersoll and Rooney)
